chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah, from Abi Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him say:

A man came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I performed Dhahr with my wife.' He said: 'Go and free a slave.' He said: 'I do not have [the means].' He said: 'Go and fast two consecutive months.' He said: 'I cannot endure it.' He said: 'Go and feed sixty poor people.' He said: 'I do not have [the means].' He said: 'Then the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'I will provide the ransom for you.' He said: 'And by He who sent you as a prophet with the truth, I do not know anyone between her two breasts (i.e., her parents/relatives) who is more in need of it than I and my dependents.' He said: 'Go, eat, and feed your dependents.'

key_terms.بَيْنَ لَبَتَيْهَا: Between her two breasts (idiom for parents/relatives)

ai.seo_question: What is the step-by-step expiation for Dhahr if one cannot afford to free a slave or fast?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the graduated expiation (*kaffarah*) for *Dhahr*, emphasizing the Prophet’s practical flexibility when the companion declined his offer to pay, prioritizing the family's immediate sustenance. It highlights the Shia scholarly view that the final stage of feeding the poor can be adapted to the individual's capacity, as demonstrated by the Prophet's instruction for the man to feed his own dependents when he asserted their greater need. This incident underscores the balance between legal obligation and compassionate discretion in marital jurisprudence.
